Assembly Bill 1346, signed by Gov. Newsom on October 9, declared that small, off-road engines (SOREs), primarily used in lawn and garden equipment, emit high levels of air pollutants including oxides of nitrogen and reactive organic gases. The new law was introduced by Assemblymembers Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park) and Lorena Gonzalez (D-San Diego) in response to projections that smog-forming pollution from gas-powered lawn equipment will surpass that from passenger cars this year. Zero-emission equivalents to all SORE equipment, like leaf-blowers and lawn-mowers, are available; cities like Palo Alto, Lomita, and Piedmont all created policy to ban the use of gas-powered lawn equipment in favor of cleaner solutions. That was back in the 90’s; at the time, jurisdictions were attracted to the ban not just for environmental purposes, but also in the interest of noise reduction. articles.text: On October 7, public health officials from all eight Bay Area counties announced that indoor mask mandates may be lifted if case rate and vaccination criteria are met. Alameda County Public Health Department estimates that this could occur in mid to late-December. In order to lift the indoor mask requirement, Alameda County must have 80% of its population fully-vaccinated and Alameda County Health Officers must deem COVID-19 hospitalizations as “low and stable.” As of October 18, 83% of Alameda County’s residents were fully vaccinated. The mandate may be lifted by mid-December, assuming that “at least some 5 to 11-year-old residents are fully vaccinated after December 10.” Hospitalization rates must continue to decline in the county, and the public health agency warned that a late fall or early winter surge could slow progress. According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 90% of ICU beds at Kaiser Hospital in Oakland are occupied, and at least 70% of ICU beds at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital are occupied as of October 18. On the same day, Alameda County entered the “moderate,” or “yellow” level of community transmission according to the Center for Disease Control tracker, meaning that COVID-19 community transmission is no longer considered “widespread.” Meeting the yellow level of community transmission is another benchmark that public health officials consider when lifting indoor mask mandates. Most Bay Area jurisdictions re-instated their indoor mask mandates in August, following a summer surge in COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. “Masks and vaccines together have protected residents of Alameda County and the Bay Area during the summer wave,” confirmed Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Officer. “While we expect COVID-19 and flu to circulate this winter, with more people well-protected from severe illness by vaccination we will be able to loosen mask requirements safely.” Marin County is currently the closest Bay Area county to discontinuing the mask mandate. Marin County Public Health Director Dr. Matt Willis said the earliest date the indoor mask mandate could end is November 3. Marin County’s population is at least 80% vaccinated as of October 18, and its hospitalization rate, or number of occupied hospital beds, is lower than Alameda County’s. As of October 18, 87% of ICU beds at Kaiser Foundation Hospital in San Rafael are occupied, and 55% of ICU beds at Marin Health Medical Center in Greenbrae are occupied. For now, Alameda County’s Health Officer Order mandating masking indoors is still in effect. Regardless of vaccination status, residents must wear masks indoors at any public setting, business, government office, and workplaces unless actively eating or drinking. The county’s public health agency also strongly recommends that unvaccinated and not fully-vaccinated individuals wear a mask in outdoor, crowded settings. Staff Photo Alameda County may lift its mandate for masks to be worn at stadiums, businesses, malls, and other crowded indoor venues if it meets hospitalization and vaccination criteria.
articles.title: County to drop mask requirement by Dec. if vaccination, hospitalization criteria met

articles.text: The League of Women Voters will host a virtual town hall style meeting on Thursday, November 4, to describe plans and progress of the new Piedmont Pool. Audience members are invited to ask Project Manager George Sanen questions about the process thus far. The meeting will highlight Piedmont’s plans for the new community pool. In November 2020, voters approved $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance a new pool that will replace the aging 3 pools. The current pools were closed permanently on September 8 one year ago. The new pool complex is scheduled to be completed prior to the summer of 2024. The Nov. 4 meeting will include brief presentations from the “city’s team”, to be followed by a question-and-answer session moderated by League of Women Voters President Lorrel Plimier. Guest speakers include Sanen, Special Assistant to the City Administrator Paul Benoit, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Register online at lwvpiedmont.org/events to receive an email with the Zoom link information. This program will be recorded and can be viewed live or at a later date on the League of Women Voters Piedmont YouTube channel.
articles.title: Town hall meeting Nov. 4 on Piedmont Pool to be virtual

These goals are aligned with measures in Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, which aim to reduce emissions from high global warming potential gases, including those from gas-powered leaf blowers and lawn mowers.” Dykman added that California’s plan to prohibit the sale of new gas-powered leaf blowers, lawn mowers, and other off-road engines further reflects the state’s commitment to providing residents cleaner air and a healthier quality of life, as well as addressing the climate crisis. “The new ban also builds on the Governor’s Executive Order banning the sale of new gas-powered vehicles by 2035. Together, these laws will help accelerate the necessary shift towards electrification, an area Piedmont is familiar with based on its decades long gas-powered leaf blower ban and recently adopted reach codes,” she said. But there are even more sustainable solutions than what the recent legislation offers, said Piedmont Resident and Piedmont Connect member Margaret Ovenden. “I think the real solution is to stop getting rid of leaves in the first place,” she said. “We have this idea that they are messy and don’t belong in our outdoors environment, but having layers of leaves on the ground is actually important for our rapidly decreasing insect populations, as mulch for the soil, etc. Leaf blowing didn’t even become a thing until recent decades. Let the leaves lie where they fall!” “The night cleaning lady has been leaving us some great investment tips.”

articles.text: Annie Wensley, Piedmont new Civic Sparks fellow. The City of Piedmont welcomed Annie Wensley as its new Civic Spark Climate Action Fellow on September 20. Wensley will work with the city’s Planning Department on climate action initiatives and other sustainability projects. Wensley graduated from Barnard College of Columbia University in New York City with a Bachelor’s degree in history, with concentrations in political science and women’s leadership studies. Prior to joining Piedmont, she worked as an Americorps Member with the National Park Service’s Student Conservation Association. Wensley was also an organizer for Kamala Harris for the People in 2019, where she recruited, trained and managed over 50 volunteers. Wensley said that the opportunities for public outreach on sustainability matters attracted her to her current position in Piedmont. One of the first tasks was to assist with the city’s free compost giveaway on September 18 at the Corporation Yard. The event was so successful the city is hosting another free giveaway this Saturday. “What I’m passionate about in regards to sustainability and environmental policy are community outreach and engagement, and climate action plan implementation,” she said. “Those two things really drew me to the city.” Wensley added that she wanted to work where there is a strong sense of community. Most recently, she and her family lived in University Place near Seattle. She chose to study at Barnard College in New York City because of its strong environmental policy program but was attracted to Piedmont because of its small size and sense of community. Wensley’s academic and professional background show a connection between environmental and social activism. “An important part of environmental movements is environmental justice, something we focused a lot on during our Civic Spark training. What drew me to [the Fellowship] is that it really focuses on capacity-building and what a Fellow can do in a year – not to just work on projects, but to help an agency like Piedmont’s local government gain the skills needed to move forward with [climate action] projects,” she said. The Civic Spark Fellowship is 11 months in which fellows serve an average of 40 hours per week. Each year, fellows work nationwide on over 100 capacity-building initiatives to help public agencies and local governments equip themselves with the resources to better respond to climate, water, housing, and mobility needs. “We are excited to have Annie on board and eager to continue to work towards our Climate Action goals,” said Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. Cammell recently returned from Florence, Italy where she studied ancient methods on how to gild glass with gold inlay, called traditional Florentine water gilding. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout office announced this week that Ellen Maloney Ruhe has been named as its new District Executive with responsibility for working with council and unit volunteers to deliver Scout programs to the youth currently in Scouting. “I enjoy the people that non-profits attract,” said Maloney Ruhe. “They are motivated to help and uplift their peers, are inspired to do good work for a common goal, and value equality and diversity in the workplace. articles.text: The Piedmont boys’ water polo team easily won back-toback matches last week, defeating San Leandro 17-10 on Tuesday, October 12, and beating Alhambra 15-7 in Martinez on Friday, October 15. The pair of wins pushes their record to 14-3 as they head into the first round of the league tournament next Tuesday, October 26. The league finals will be played on Saturday, October 30. Sophomore Peter Krumins had a huge week with six goals against Alhambra and five against San Leandro. He continues to be a standout first-year varsity player. Senior captain Antonio Rivera, meanwhile, scored three goals and four assists against San Leandro and put in another two against Alhambra. 17-10 win vs. San Leandro Piedmont came out strong in the first quarter to lead 6-1 and jumped to a 10-6 by halftime. In the third quarter, the Highlanders’ defense held strong to extend the advantage 12-6. PHS added five goals in the fourth, 17-10. Griffin Stein scored the game’s opening goal after 30 seconds while Krumins got his first with 4:54 left in the opening period. A Rivera goal made it 3-1 with 3:26 on the clock, and Krumins scored on a penalty shot with 1:36 left. Rivera made it 5-1 with a minute left, while George Stein extended the lead to 6-1 with a heave with 2 seconds on the clock. But the Pirates stunned the Highlanders by powering back to tie the game at 6-6 with 2:47 left in the first half. Piedmont responded with four unanswered goals; Krumins rocketed one in with 2:40 to go, followed by George Stein’s second goal after 21 seconds, 8-6. Krumins added an insurance goal with 1:39 left, and Rivera closed out the first al scoring on a penalty shot with 34 seconds left. In the third quarter, Piedmont turned up the defensive pressure and allowed no goals by the Pirates, They took a 12-6 lead on goals by Rivera and Stein. In the fourth quarter, PHS scored five more goals, and allowed four by San Leandro. Declan Linnane scored after 20 seconds, and made the game 14-7 with 6:11 to go. Shane Miller scored with 5:24 remaining, then Rivera made it 16-8 with 4:59 on the clock. While Griffin Stein scored the final goal of the game, 17-10, with 30 seconds remaining. Final stats: Krumins scored five goals; Rivera had three goals, four assists, and two steals; George Stein had three goals and a steal; Griffin Stein had two goals; Linnane had two goals, one assist, and two steals. articles.text: Piedmont Homecoming game this Friday vs. O’Dowd Playing in Alameda on Friday, October 15, the Highlanders came up one touchdown short against the Encinal Jets, 34-28 loss. “It’s always the little things; maybe missing keys or some confusion in calling the correct play we sent in, or balls over the top just unable to knock them down. If we execute on those one or two little plays, they change the game. We are always right at the door, we just need to kick it open,” said Piedmont football coach Jerome Johnson. The Highlanders were able to keep the game deadlocked 14-14 at halftime, but allowed 20 points in the third quarter and trailed 34-21 heading into the last quarter. Piedmont’s final touchdown came with 1:38 left in the game, leading to an onside kick attempt to try to regain possession. Despite the loss, receiver Nico Defazio had another big game with 192 total yards of offense, 130 on pass receptions, including two touchdowns, and 62 yards rushing. Senior quarterback Adhi Bornstein completed 13 of 27 passes for three touchdowns. He was also intercepted three times in the second varsity start of his high school career. Playing cornerback on defense, he intercepted an Encinal pass. Game Recap Piedmont gave up a fumble on the opening possession at their own 35-yard line, resulting in a 65 yard touchdown run on Encinal’s first possession. But Piedmont responded quickly with a long offensive possession that ended with a 30-yard pass over the middle to Defazio in the end zone. He leaped over his defender to make the catch with seven minutes left in the first quarter. Piedmont’s defense did well to force a three-and-out on Encinal’s next possession and began at their own 44-yard line. However, a quarterback sack and fumble on the first play put the Jets in position to go ahead. PHS was able to force a 4th-and-10 for Encinal from the 28, but the Jets scored on a pass for a 14-7 lead with 3:14 left in the first quarter. Defazio returned the kickoff 20 yards to the PHS 48-yard line. The Highlanders worked the ball to the Jets’ 45 when Bornstein connected on a bomb to Ryan McConathy for the touchdown to tie Encinal 14-14. PHS forced a punt on Encinal’s next possession, but the Jets intercepted Piedmont at the Highlanders’ 32 yard line with 7:46 left in the second quarter. Piedmont’s defense stood stout, preventing Encinal from converting a 4th-and-6 at the 18-yard-line with 5:30 to go. The score remained tied at 14-14 at halftime. articles.text: The JV Highlanders had their strongest game of the season on Friday, October 15, crushing the Encinal Jets 39-6 in Alameda. Receiver Sam Shelby led the way with four touchdowns. Quarterback Marcos Lagios returned to the starting lineup after missing time. Encinal opened the game with a kickoff return for a touchdown, but it was its only score in the game. “It was nice to have Marcos back. We knew he was going to be ready, so we really wanted to let it rip. Encinal scored on the opening kickoff and that was it. We shut them down [after that],” said offensive coordinator Bradley Smet. Piedmont answered quickly on its first possession. Starting at the 30-yard line, the Scots scored on its first play from scrimmage by speedy receiver Sam Shelby, who scored on a 70-yard pass play. An extra point by Shelby made the score 7-6. On the Jets’ next possession, Piedmont’s Brandon Dicke recovered a fumble at Encinal’s 20-yard line, setting up running back Tommy Ashton for a shortyard touchdown run to put PHS ahead 13-6. Piedmont’s defense then forced a turnover on Encinal’s next possession when Cash Elmquist hurried the quarterback into an bad pass. Jordan Alemania intercepted the ball near the Jets’ end zone. It took just one play for quarterback Lagios to find Shelby on a touchdown pass and a 20-6 lead. Shelby scored twice more to guarantee a big win for the Scots. Piedmont‘s final points were scored with four minutes left in the game for the 39-6 final. articles.text: Filoli terrace lights Filoli House and Garden in Woodside announced on October 6 a compensation structure based on the living wage for San Mateo County residents. Filoli’s new compensation plan for all employees, included in its 2019-2023 strategic plan, is based on a model created in 2004 by Dr. Amy Glasmeier of M.I.T. According to the calculations, the living wage in San Mateo County is $28 per hour for fulltime employees. Filoli, a nonprofit, cited the lack of a true, geographically-specific living wage information, and the fact that San Mateo County is the third most expensive place to live in America. “It’s an ethical imperative,” Filoli CEO Kara Newport said. “If we want to attract and retain a diverse staff reflective of our community, we have to pay a living wage. The Filoli experience is dependent on people, so the quality of employees matters.” Newport stated that Filoli cannot be equitable in practice without regional pay equity. In February, Filoli launched a Diversity, Equity, Accessibility and Inclusion (DEAI) Policy and Action Plan centered around the importance of investing in its employees. President of the Board David Wollenberg explained that Filoli has “a staff of over 60 people… and we want to keep them all.” The cost of living adjustment follows a series of benefits the nonprofit added in recent years, which included doubling the organization’s employee 401k match, adding additional holidays and personal time off, a sabbatical program, and education reimbursement.
articles.title: Filoli announces Living Wage Program for all full-time employees

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes Angelique Kidjo as the organization’s first season-long artist-in-residence. She will perform her unique take on the Talking Head’s 1980 album Remain in Light on Friday, October 29 at Zellerbach Hall. “One of the great pleasures this season is welcoming Angélique Kidjo, who hasn’t appeared here in nearly a decade, back to Berkeley as our first season-long artist-in-residence,” said Jeremy Geffen, Cal Performances Artistic Director. “Having been a presenter, collaborator and fan of her work for years, I know firsthand of her passion, conviction, and boundless curiosity. She brings inextinguishable energy—more so than most of her more junior colleagues, actually—to bear in both her performances and her community outreach work.” Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and was recently named one of Time Magazine’s “100 most influential people of 2021” for her work in the arts and as a cultural ambassador. The artist fled a dictatorship in her home country of Benin and draws from ,, her personal experiences when creating music. Kidjo’s latest recording, Mother Nature, was released earlier this year and incorporates West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. “Angélique draws from her personal experiences a deep sense of conviction as well as profound passion for exploring the breadth and depth of the human experience—qualities that make her the perfect partner for our season-long Illuminations programming. And most importantly, she comes to our campus hoping to learn as much as to share,” Geffen said. “By inviting her to meet with faculty and students, Cal Performances reinforces and supports the university’s values of cultivating and sustaining a diverse, equitable, informed, and inclusive and accessible community.” The concert begins at 8 p.m. on Friday, October 29 in Zellerbach Hall on the University of California campus. Tickets are $36 to $96. Half-price tickets are available for UC Berkeley students. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, at calperformances. org, and at the door. Proof of a COVID-19 vaccination is required for entry. articles.text: Thomas (Blind Tom) Higgins was a prodigy. a virtuosic pianist, gifted composer, and one of the most in-demand musicians of his time in America. The most sensational career in recent memory began in 1958 when American pianist Van Cliburn won the first Tchaikovsky competition in Moscow. Remember that this was the height of the Cold War. The Russian judges did not know what to do, so they asked premier Nikita Khrushchev. All Khrushchev asked was: “Is he the best?” The judges said he was. Khrushchev said: “Give him first prize.” Another sensational career was begun when Leonard Bernstein substituted for an ailing conductor for a concert in Carnegie Hall. The rest, as they say, is history. Any violinist who won first prize at the Paris Conservatory was guaranteed an international career. Pablo de Sarasate was only one of many. And then there was the career of a pianist named Thomas Wiggins. His biography reads like the most sensational Hollywood movie. Thomas was born into slavery in 1849. He was also born blind. What I’m going to tell you might sound very strange, but his blindness turned out to be something of a blessing. Wiggins gained fame if not fortune as “Blind Tom”. Since he was born blind, he was unable to work in any capacity. He heard music in his youngest years and soon was playing the piano in an extraordinary manner. The little kid would hear any tune and play it back perfectly. Not long after this, he became the property of a certain General Bethune. The Civil War ended that situation, but the general envisioned a great financial future in “Blind Tom”. The general was a great promoter and marketed Blind Tom as the “genius of the age”. Remember that Blind Tom could play just about any tune he heard. The publicity ranged from genius to savant. It didn’t really matter to the general what the publicity said as long as he made money. And Blind Tom was a very marketable quantity. The amount of money he reportedly made was staggering. It also seems that the general, was an exploiter of the first order. How much money was passed on to Wiggins is debatable. One may assume that Tom was given a pittance. But how good was Blind Tom as a musician? They say that he composed some 7000 pieces, an unprecedented number. After listening to a few of his pieces, I discovered that they range from the exquisitely beautiful to bombastic. Once again, I ask you not to jump to conclusions. One of his compositions is entitled the “Battle of Manassas.” It is somewhat akin to Louis Moreau Gottschalk’s famous composition “The Union”. Blind Tom probably had never heard Gottschalk play the piano, and his composition is innovative in the extreme. Other people wrote battle music, so why not “The Battle of Manassas” by Blind Tom? It amazes me how he could even conceive a piece like this. How did he even learn about the sounds of battle? All of this was of great interest to me. I have never had the opportunity of hearing any music by this historical figure. But the ever-enterprising pianist Carl Blake performed two of Thomas Wiggins’ piano pieces on Sunday in San Francisco. He chose “Oliver Gallop” and “Reve Charmant”. Both pieces are thoroughly American and combine the pianistic panache of Gottschalk tempered with the melodic touch of Verdi. Carl Blake played these pieces with uncommon sensitivity and a beautiful tone. Maybe next time he will play “The Battle of Manassas”. To some Blind Tom was a heavily marketed curiosity; a savant of extraordinary dimensions who made a fortune for his exploiter… er …manager. I prefer to think of Thomas Wiggins as a fascinating talent. In many ways he was like the immortal jazz pianist Art Tatum, who was nearly blind. And that ain’t bad.

articles.text: Sound out the trumpets, Beethoven is back in operatown! They did right by Beethoven at the S.F. Opera, staging his only (and foresightedly heroic) opera Fidelio nearly a year after his 250th birthday, with Covid19 acting as the black-hat hold-up man at the War Memorial Opera House. If the performance was a bit spotty, no matter. The key word was revolutionary, his message of freedom and individuals bucking repression and suppression by corrupt authorities. And how revolutionary it was in 1805 to have a woman disguising herself as a man and prison guard to do the heroic deed, freeing the political prisoner Florestan, opera’s first great freedom fighter, at great personal risk. Their also being married leads to expressions of love and a grand public celebration in the finale’s music, foreshadowing the epic “Ode to Joy” still locked up for years in the mind and quill of the ill-fated composer Ludwig van Beethoven, who became stone deaf early on and left us at age 55. Given all the political prisoners around the world in today’s news, this opera is more than relevant. The opera showed the composer in transition, starting off with a traditional, low-key German Singspiel work (related to the mode of Mozart’s Magic Flute) and erupting in huge vocal outpourings and high drama of the future, with its passion bleeding into the rich score. It’s as if the last act were written some decades after the first. If you were expecting huge Wagnerian voices again in the two leads the other night, recall that when this opera appeared, Wagnerian voices were not yet cultivated and Richard Wagner himself not yet born. Slow starting, soprano Elsa van den Heever was effective and vibrantly hall-filling in the final scenes as Leonore, the opera’s main character (called Fidelio in her male guard’s disguise). The low male voices were admirable, from Greer Grimsley’s Pizarro to Soloman Howard’s Fernando to James Creswell’s Rocco. The best German of the night in the spoken passages came from Grimsley and Creswell. The supertitle translations softened the text, changing Rocco’s “Gold” aria dripping with greed to a mild discourse on the importance of money in this world. Tenor Russell Thomas’ Florestan fared best in the ensembles. He was hampered by his confinement, in a lower-depths dungeon, seated in a golden chair worthy for a monarch. Tilt! Overall, conductor Eun Sun Kim’s best moments came in leading the various trios and quartets by the principals as well as in holding together the massed crowds of the finale. Notable was how her orchestra brought out the surge within Pizarro’s arietta (act two, scene one), where similarities had you swearing that Beethoven was extremely familiar with the hell-scene finale of Mozart’s Don Giovanni. Kim’s keeping the orchestra and singers in sync worked intermittently. More control over the brass section and a bit more rehearsal would have been welcome. If you like contemporary production with modern structures, TVs and cell phones, this is your show, with the two-story rotating set by Alexander V. Nichols clearly the big attention-getter. Some corners had been cut out of pandemic necessity, where the warehouse-like structure hardly suggested a dungeon nor the depths for digging Florestan’s intended grave. Also cut in part was some of the dated dialogue, but uncut was the curiously bifurcated Beethoven score, a unique gem handed down, as Fidelio was his only such venture. Opera fans were already regretting the impending 2022 retirement of Choral Director Ian Robertson, who shaped the awe-inspired (Male) Prisoners Chorus in act one and the augmented fortissimo mixed chorus of the finale. Matthew Ozawa served as Stage Director. MUSIC NOTES Audiences were still euphoric about the resumption of an indoor opera season, after Tosca and Fidelio, both assembled under rather arduous conditions of pandemic which, among other things, inhibited importing foreign singers because of constantly varying Covid regulations everywhere… After Gustav Mahler’s innovation, countless theaters inserted the great “Leonore Overture No. 3” and played it between the last two scenes while stagehands laboriously converted from dungeon to open-air mass celebration. No such interpolation here, because the scene change is instantaneous (i.e., no curtain) with the rotating set…. The message of Fidelio is viewed as highly symbolic around the world; it was chosen to reopen major theaters in Vienna and Budapest in the past century after times of deprivation. Concurrent with the opera, reactivation has reopened the Ira Brilliant Center for Beethoven Studies at San Jose State University Wednesday to Friday afternoons. It has the largest music collection of Beethoven first editions anywhere outside of Germany. Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, in German with supertitle translations by San Francisco Opera. Two acts, one intermission, 2.5 hours. Performing October 14-30 at War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco. Masks and Vaxx required for all. For info: (415) 864-3330 or go online. www.sfopera.com

articles.text: Lucas Hedges, Shia LaBeouf and Noah Jupe (front) star in Honey Boy. Honey Boy is a raw, gritty, semi-autobiographical film, written by Shia LaBeouf and revealing a period in his life when he was living in a seedy L.A. motel with his father, who he names James Lort (LaBeouf). His two alter-ego characters are 12-year-old Otis (Noah Jupe), a child actor, and the twenty-something, Otis (Chris Hedges) who has become a self-destructive movie star ordered into rehab by a judge. It’s in rehab, during sessions with a therapist, that Otis tells his story in a series of long flashbacks. The year is 1995. James is not so much a father as a man locked in perpetual battle with his own demons, while young Otis struggles to avoid becoming collateral damage. James – an alcoholic, ex-con, veteran, and former rodeo clown – riffs and rants and rages, his verbal abuse of Otis on occasion turns physical. Their interaction pretty much takes place in the confines of their motel room, usually before James takes Otis to the set on his motorcycle or in the evening when they have returned to their claustrophobic room. James is ostensibly managing Otis’ career as a child star acting in B-movies. And while Otis is on set, James attends AA meetings, veterans therapy groups, or plants rows of marijuana along a nearby freeway. Their dysfunctional relationship is that of father and son; however, it’s also one in which the son assumes the role of the reasonable adult and the father becomes the unreasonable child. There are times when Otis hates his father, the man who has exposed him to alcohol, weed, and cigarettes, seems to relish denigrating him while demeaning the size of his pre-adolescent penis. He meets and then tosses Otis’ Big Brother/mentor into the motel pool. He often rides off on his Harley, leaving Otis to spend long nights fending for himself. But then Otis also loves his father, craves his attention, and wants above all to be wrapped in his arms and protected. Regardless, James seems only intent on transferring to Otis – a lonely, precocious boy – the gnarled and twisted damage likely visited upon him. articles.text: The White Ribbon, is a German film nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, and winner of the top prize (Palm d’Or) at Cannes. Directed by Michael Haneke (Cache).It is artful, superbly cast, and beautifully photographed in stark black and white. The year is 1913, on the cusp of World War I. The film opens with a lovely shot of farmers and villagers harvesting the summer wheat, followed by a celebration heralding the end of one season and the beginning of another. It’s tempting to romanticize this bucolic setting, a small town surrounded by the flat expanse of rural northern Germany, filled with hardworking people whose lives follow the rhythms of the land. But then Haneke grimly pulls back a curtain and reveals that behind this seemingly benign image is a bleak and cruel reality that is astonishing in its severity. There is no overt violence in the film except for a set piece in the first minutes when a doctor, riding home on his horse, is brought down by an all but invisible trip wire. At first the incident, called an accident, seems an aberration. But then other events take place of equal premeditation, testimony to the fact that a malevolent and mysterious perpetrator resides in the village. Though these chilling acts of violence are linchpins throughout the film, what is far more disturbing is the authoritarian, patriarchal cruelty leveled against the village’s children. The adults, charged with loving them, are so consistently perverse in their anger and punishments that it’s as if we’re watching and exorcism of their childhood innocence and innate empathy, carried out with an endemic ignorance and righteousness and malice that is disturbing to watch. The village Pastor, blinded by his own narrow Protestantism, in a particularly unsettling scene ties white ribbons around the arms of his children as reminders that they have violated his trust, betrayed their purity, and disappointed their parents. He will not remove the ribbons until they have demonstrated that they are pure once again. The ribbons torment the children and are reminders of the hypocrisy and heartlessness of those adults to whom the children look for protection and, yes, love. The f ilm also answers Haneke’s own question: is the heart of man inherently dark, absent any overriding humanity that will act as a counterbalance to evil? His answer is, in frame after frame, an unequivocal yes. He also asks the audience to extrapolate from the microcosm of this small village to the fascism that eventually gripped all of Germany in which millions were killed because of a reflexive response to the uber-fascist-father, Hitler, who turned Germany into a gnarled and pathological nation not dissimilar from the village nor the acts perpetrated against the children. To contemplate The White Ribbon is to feel both revulsion and admiration. Overly long (almost 2-1/2 hours), unrelentingly dour and forbidding, it is also unfailingly honest regarding the ability of one generation to do great harm to the next. For some, this film will be more than they want to endure. Others will watch in fascination while acknowledging that Haneke is a superb filmmaker. The White Ribbon. Starring Christian Friedel, Leonie Benesch, Urich Tukur and Ursina Lardi. Directed by Michael Haneke. 2 hrs., 24 min. Rated R.

articles.text: The Incredibles, Pixar’s film about a family of superheroes. The Incredibles is a stylized, computer-generated action toon starring a family of under-the-radar superheroes. The patriarch of what will soon be a family of five is Mr. Incredible (Craig T. Nelson), a popular superhero, beloved by all for his rescues, foiled bank robberies, and suicide interventions. But despite his passion for what he does, the public grows weary of the collateral damage that occurs with each rescue. As a result, he and his new wife, Elastic Girl (Holly Hunter), are forced into what is called the Superhero Relocation Program, and are required to live normal lives, using the names Bob and Helen Parr. Flash forward 15 years. Bob is an insurance salesman, and he and Helen have three children – Dash (Spencer Fox), Violet (Sarah Vowell), and baby Jack Jack. As it turns out, Bob is growing increasingly dissatisfied with his mundane life. He yearns for the good old days when he was Mr. Incredible, and reminisces each day on the way to work while stuck in traffic with Lucius, aka Mr. Frozone (Samuel L. Jackson), while they listen to a police scanner. Both are tempted to help out the cops when they can. One day, a mysterious woman named Mirage (Elizabeth Pena) appears and makes them a job offer. Bob seizes the opportunity to return to his role as Mr. Incredible. He is convinced that like those days of yesteryear, he can make a difference. But he soon runs into an archenemy called Syndrome (Jason Lee). It doesn’t take long before Mr. Incredible’s whole family is involved in running battles and action chases with this nemesis. The Incredibles is one of Pixar’s best, a wonderful example of high-tech animation, lushly created backgrounds, slap-dash humor and jokes, with superhero costumes and signature masks. The kids will love it, as will the adults. The Incredibles, Computer animated. Directed and co-written by Brad Bird. With voices of Craig T. Nelson, Holly Hunter, Samuel L. Jackson. Pixar/Walt Disney. 1 hr., 55 min, Rated PG.

If the male’s song matches the female’s’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. articles.text: Throughout the City of Piedmont, residents, businesses, and schools participate in three-container “source separated” waste collections. While Piedmonters are familiar with blue recycling, green organics, and black garbage carts, some residents may not understand why waste collection is separated in this way or how this method of collection advances Piedmont’s climate action goals. In particular, residents often have questions about organic waste. Organic waste is constituted of recovered products such as food scraps, green material, yard trimmings (landscape and pruning waste), untreated wood, and food-soiled paper products. When collected and processed on a significant scale, organic waste can be recycled into new products such as compost, mulch, biofuel, and electricity. In Piedmont organic waste is collected by Republic Services and converted into mulch and compost. While there are two significant methods of composting – backyard or home composting and commercial or industrial composting – the collection of green organic waste carts is part of the cycle of commercial and industrial composting. Industrial composting facilities are designed to effectively process large volumes of municipal and commercial organic waste. In turn, this compost can be sold back to landscapers, farmers, and plant nurseries in a circular, self-sustaining process. Not only can the product of large-scale composting advance California’s green economy, but with new regulations beginning in 2022, jurisdictions will begin procuring recycled organic material and making it available to residents. These new regulations, set forth in the California state legislation (Senate Bill 1383), were signed into law in 2016 in a statewide effort to reduce emissions of short-lived climate pollutants. The connection between compost and greenhouse gas emissions comes from the emission of methane gas from organic waste in landfills. Methane gas, which is a super pollutant that is over 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over the course of 20 years, is emitted when organic waste such as food scraps, wood, and paper decompose in landfills. As the single largest waste stream and the source of 20 percent of methane emissions in California, diverting organic waste to become compost can significantly reduce the state’s emissions. California’s new regulations support environmental initiatives at the core, while benefiting our communities and spaces and improving soil and air quality, all on both a state and local level. Piedmonters can benefit firsthand from the proper disposal of their own organic waste by collecting compost from the City’s free compost giveaway events. The City’s next compost giveaway is this Saturday, October 23 from 9:00am-12:00pm at the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. As Halloween celebrations draw closer, don’t forget to support the Piedmont community’s local schools at the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch at Coaches Field this year. pages.text: Wednesday, October 20, 2021 23 By Annie Wensley Throughout the City of Piedmont, residents, businesses, and schools participate in three-container “source separated” waste collections. While Piedmonters are familiar with blue recycling, green organics, and black garbage carts, some residents may not understand why waste collection is separated in this way or how this method of collection advances Piedmont’s climate action goals. In particular, residents often have questions about organic waste. Organic waste is constituted of recovered products such as food scraps, green material, yard trimmings (landscape and pruning waste), untreated wood, and food-soiled paper products. When collected and processed on a significant scale, organic waste can be recycled into new products such as compost, mulch, biofuel, and electricity. In Piedmont organic waste is collected by Republic Services and converted into mulch and compost. While there are two significant methods of composting – backyard or home composting and commercial or industrial composting – the collection of green organic waste carts is part of the cycle of The Dirt on Compost commercial and industrial composting. Industrial composting facilities are designed to effectively process large volumes of municipal and commercial organic waste. In turn, this compost can be sold back to landscapers, farmers, and plant nurseries in a circular, self-sustaining process. Not only can the product of large-scale composting advance California’s green economy, but with new regulations beginning in 2022, jurisdictions will begin procuring recycled organic material and making it available to residents. These new regulations, set forth in the California state legislation (Senate Bill 1383), were signed into law in 2016 in a statewide effort to reduce emissions of short-lived climate pollutants. The connection between compost and greenhouse gas emissions comes from the emission of methane gas from organic waste in landfills. Methane gas, which is a super pollutant that is over 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over the course of 20 years, is emitted when organic waste such as food scraps, wood, and paper decompose in landfills. As the single largest waste stream and the source of 20 percent of methane emissions in California, diverting organic waste to become compost can significantly reduce the state’s emissions. California’s new regulations support environmental initiatives at the core, while benefiting our communities and spaces and improving soil and air quality, all on both a state and local level. articles.text: State-of-the-art renovation includes new NASA Ames Visitor Center A rendering of the new NASA Ames Visitor Center at the Chabot Space & Science Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will reopen Friday, November 12 with a new NASA Ames Visitor Center, following more than 18 months of closure to complete construction on the largest project since 2000. “Chabot is kicking off an exciting next chapter to re-envision science education in partnership with NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, making visible the extraordinary people and legacy of discovery at NASA,” said Chabot Executive Director Adam Tobin. The NASA Experience will feature some fascinating items in space research and exploration, including spacesuits from the Mercury and Gemini missions, experimental heat shield technology, and a fan blade from the world’s largest wind tunnel. Many of these items have never been on display to the public. Visitors will get to step into the role of a NASA scientist by embarking on hands-on activities and connecting with NASA scientists in interactive stations. Guests will be able to design and build rovers, planes, and space robots for exploration, then test them in extraordinary environments inspired by labs at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Chabot Space & Science Center will celebrate its reopening weekend with three days of festivities with extended hours to accommodate demand. Tickets will be limited, and visitors are encouraged to buy their timed tickets in advance. The weekend will include researchers and scientists from NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View, including astronaut Dr. Yvonne Cagle. Additionally, the weekend will include performances and workshops with community partners, a space-themed collaborative build zone, and robotics demonstrations by teen Galaxy Explorers. About Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and planet Earth. Chabot’s hours are 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Chabotspace.org 10000 Skyline Blvd, Oakland, (510) 336-7300.

The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered for its weekly walk on October 13 with 26 walkers and one K-9 best friend. The group was especially happy to welcome first-time walkers Kathy Marks, Pat Keller, Maulshree Solanki, and Dena Belinkoff. Priscilla Wanerus announced that Jane Leroe, a retired lawyer and longtime Mt. View Cemetery docent, would be leading a tour of the historic cemetery on October 27 – just in time for Halloween. As part of its goal of visiting every safe Piedmont street each year, the group decided to target the little-traveled streets below Wildwood School in the southwest section of Piedmont. They began on the one-way, lower part of Wildwood Avenue. The upper part of the same street is two ways, making Wildwood very unusual. The group came to the Four-W intersection of Wildwood, Winsor, Warfield Avenues, and Wallace Road. At Boulevard Way the walkers turned right and went down to Grand Avenue, crossing into Oakland. On the way they came upon a yard with an expansive, beautiful garden covered with cactus and other drought resistant plants, and a stately palm tree at the top of the yard. Near the bottom of Boulevard is an alley, the almost invisible Sylvan Way, where they a newly remodeled now modern home, and more Halloween decorations. The end of the block-long street presented a challenge, where it takes a 90-degree left turn to a very steep hill that ends on Wildwood Avenue. Wildwood quickly became Palm Drive, so named for the palm trees that early 19th Century Piedmont developer Frank C. Havens planted as the entrance to Piedmont Park. The group went up Wallace Road, a one-way street coming down, and passed the “Camel House” at the corner of Winsor, another home with a personal history. Turning left, they went down Winsor to Park View Avenue, which is at the base of Witter Field and another new street for the group where they saw many more ghosts, spiders, and skeletons on the homes. Park View ends at Magnolia Avenue, where the group turned right and went back uphill to their starting place at the Exedra. On the way they had one more opportunity to visit a seldom visited street, Larmer Court, a cul-desac with three homes. Does any other Piedmont street have fewer homes, they wondered. Even Cavendish Lane on the Oakland border near Park Boulevard has four Piedmont homes. It had been a fun, three-mile walk in less than 90 minutes; filled with seldom seen streets, unique homes and gardens, Halloween house decorations, social equity reminders, sounds of happy children, and good conversations with new and old Wednesday walking friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Respite care is when a family caregiver is given a break – a rest or a respite – from their responsibilities caring for a loved one. This break might occur when another family member steps up for a time, or by hiring a professional caregiver to do some of the caregiving instead of the family. Many family caregivers are juggling work, caring for other family such as young children, plus a variety of tasks for someone who is physically or mentally unable to fully care for themselves due to age, illness, or disability. Sometimes it becomes too much, and in order to continue helping out at all, a break is needed. While home care is for the person who needs assistance, the respite is for the family of the client who is receiving the home care services. Why is respite care so important? The expression, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” sums up the critical need for respite care. Family caregivers can give too much of themselves in service to a loved one and damage their own health and wellbeing. When that happens, everyone needs care – medical care, home care, nursing care, you name it, depending on the circumstances. Even a weekly movie night out for a couple of hours, or a Sunday morning in church, during which time the person who needs care is tended to by another, can give someone back their own peace of mind and well-being. What does in-home care mean to you? If you are a family caregiver in need of a break, you might be wondering what a professional caregiver can step in and do in your place. A trained caregiver can be there to assist with daily bathing and grooming, become like a friend and companion to take walks and play games together, do a little light housekeeping during their visit, provide medication reminders, run some errands including those that the client may need to join, and more. Respite care is available for short and long-term care needs, whether someone is recovering from a surgery or developing additional symptoms after a diagnosis of a progressive illness. You may need respite care for a senior, or caring for a loved one of any age. Whether you seek out professional in-home care services or are asking friends and family to share the load, make sure you take breaks for yourself from time to time to maintain your wellness. Lombardi High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” By 1885, the mulberry grove was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. articles.text: A carjacking occurred on Wednesday, October 13, at 7:50 p.m. in the area of Wildwood Avenue and Prospect Road. A resident seated in a vehicle was approached by approximately five suspects, one of whom was armed with a gun. The suspects ordered the victim out of the vehicle, stole additional items belonging to the victim, and fled the area in the victim’s vehicle. A witness called 911 and Piedmont officers responded to the scene. The suspects, male juveniles wearing dark hoodies, dark pants, and COVID face masks, were not located and are currently at large. The victim was not physically harmed. Detectives are currently conducting an investigation of this incident and working with regional law enforcement partners to identify commonalities with other similar incidents in other jurisdictions. Anyone with additional information about this incident is asked to contact Detective John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015 or Detective George Tucker at (510) 420-3013. While this type of crime is rare in Piedmont, the Police Department asks the public to be aware of their surroundings and report suspicious activity related to criminal conduct in a timely manner by calling 911 for emergencies and (510) 420-3000 for non-emergency situations.

articles.text: Staff photo Mom Julianna Monin with Evelina and younger sister Ceca examine the Giant Jack pumpkin to guess its weight. Evelina considered a large number and asked if it could possibly be 150 pounds. The Giant Jack is now on display at the Wildwood Dads’ Pumpkin Patch at Coaches’ Field. The Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch will be open daily through Saturday, October 30, with plenty of time for families to stock up prior to Halloween. The pumpkin patch has a big variety of 15 types of pumpkins and gourds. In addition to traditional carving pumpkins, the patch has some specialty pumpkins, like the Knucklehead, the “One too Many,” the American Tondo and the Polar Bear pumpkin (all white). New and popular this year are the other worldly Marina Di Chioggias, the tie-die colored Turks Turbans, and a ghost-shaped Yugoslavian Finger Fruit. “We have seen families come back twice with their kids. Some of that is motivated by not really having a Halloween last year so really everyone trying to make up for it,” said Wildwood Dad Randy Wells. The Giant Jack heavyweight pumpkin is the centerpiece. For $1 kids can guess the weight of the enormous pumpkin. The person with the closest guess will win the Giant Jack with free home delivery.

Back by popular demand, the City of Piedmont, in partnership with Republic Services, is holding a free compost giveaway for residents at the City’s Corporation Yard (next to Coaches Field on Moraga Avenue) on Saturday, October 23 from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Piedmont residents may pick up to one cubic yard of compost while supplies last. Preorders are not available. Bring shovels, gloves, containers, and proof of residency (driver’s license or current Republic Services bill) to pick up compost. Residents must bag and load the compost themselves. Residents are asked to wear masks or face coverings and follow the Alameda County Public Health Department’s COVID-19 guidance. While not required, it is strongly encouraged to fill out an online form to indicate your estimated pickup time on Saturday. The form can be found at https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FAIpQLSfd-w0Sz08FIuXz38E- 2kRntXClTl60awmIhUxPmU2IThe compost is made from yard trimmings and food waste collected in curbside organics collection services. Mixing compost with your soil adds nutrients to the soil, aids in water retention and pest control, and helps plants thrive The City is also proud to support the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch, which is next to the compost pickup area. Come by to grab your free compost and support Piedmont’s local schools. You can have your pumpkin, and compost it too. For more information contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420- 3058.

articles.text: JACK ELVEKROG Football Amherst College Jack Elvekrog, PHS Class of 2019, is a sophomore fullback on the Amherst College football team. He was a leader on the Piedmont High football team as a tight end and helped lead the lacrosse team to its 2019 NCS Championship. At Amherst Elvekrog has developed as a useful member of the backfield this season, recording 31 rushing attempts for 89 yards, to go along with three pass receptions for five yards.
